analysis.one_liner: Raises food stamp benefits to a realistic food budget, eases deductions, ends a work time limit, and brings Puerto Rico into SNAP.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor action in the Senate before the 118th Congress ended, so no change was made to SNAP benefit rules.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would base monthly SNAP (food stamp) benefits on the government's "low-cost food plan" — the estimated cost of a basic healthy diet for a family of four — instead of the cheaper "thrifty food plan" used today, and raise the minimum benefit. It would give households with an elderly or disabled member a standard medical expense deduction, remove the cap on deductions for high shelter (rent/utility) costs, and end the three-month time limit on food aid for childless adults who are not meeting work requirements. It would also move Puerto Rico from its capped block grant into the regular SNAP program, with a $112.5 million grant for the technology needed to run it [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that receive SNAP. Families would see larger monthly allotments because the low-cost food plan is a more generous, realistic food budget than the thrifty plan now used. Households with elderly or disabled members would get an easier medical deduction, high-rent households would no longer have their shelter deduction capped, and childless adults between 18 and 49 would no longer lose benefits after three months if they cannot meet work requirements. Puerto Rico residents, who today receive a smaller block-grant nutrition program, would qualify for standard SNAP benefits [S2] [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Requires SNAP allotments to be calculated using the USDA low-cost food plan — the diet needed to feed a reference family of four — reevaluated every five years against current prices, replacing the cheaper thrifty food plan now used as the benefit basis [S2] [S3].
Creates a standard medical expense deduction (starting at $140, inflation-adjusted) for households with an elderly or disabled member, instead of requiring documented excess medical costs [S2] [S3].
Eliminates the cap on the excess shelter expense deduction, so families paying a large share of income in rent and utilities can deduct the full amount [S2] [S3].
Eliminates the time limit on SNAP for able-bodied adults without dependents, which currently cuts off benefits after three months of unemployment [S2] [S3].
Lets Puerto Rico join regular SNAP instead of its capped block grant, and appropriates $112.5 million for the technology infrastructure to implement it [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through higher SNAP spending: the more generous benefit basis, larger deductions, end of the time limit, and Puerto Rico's move to standard SNAP (plus the one-time $112.5 million technology grant) all raise federal costs. Grocery and food retailers receive more SNAP dollars, and state agencies administer a slightly easier set of rules [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; costs flow to grocers

drawbacks.text: The bill raises federal spending materially: the low-cost food plan is a larger food budget than the thrifty plan, the uncapped shelter deduction and new medical deduction increase benefits for many households, and Puerto Rico's transition to standard SNAP replaces a fixed block grant with open-ended federal cost, all of which draw objections in an era of deficit pressure [S2] [S3].

Ending the three-month time limit for childless adults removes the work requirement that supporters of the current rule say encourages employment; opponents argue assistance without any time limit discourages work — a long-running disagreement over SNAP's ABAWD rules [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households the bill covers, the gains are direct and concrete: fuller grocery budgets, simpler deductions, no benefit cliff after three months of unemployment. The trade-off is real federal cost — a more generous benefit formula nationwide and an uncapped Puerto Rico commitment — and the work-requirement elimination is genuinely contested. The core benefit-formula change is a straightforward correction: the thrifty food plan long understated the real cost of a basic diet, and the low-cost plan is the standard USDA benchmark closer to what families actually spend.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, read twice, and referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee in April 2023, and the committee never took it up, so it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Gillibrand introduced the bill on April 27, 2023, with seven original cosponsors (Markey, Welch, Warren, Booker, Brown, Sanders, Fetterman) [S1] [S3].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry — the last action ever taken on it [S5].
It attracted 11 cosponsors, all Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on [S4].
The Agriculture Committee held no markup, reported no vote, and the full Senate never considered it before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: SNAP households saw no benefit increase: the thrifty food plan formula, the shelter-deduction cap, the childless-adult time limit, and Puerto Rico's block grant all stayed as they were, and federal food-aid spending was not increased. Opponents of expanding SNAP kept the status quo at no political cost, since no vote ever had to be recorded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo; no SNAP changes were made

for.what_they_did: Signed on during the Congress; none were Republican [S4].

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Debbie Stabenow, D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill in the roughly 21 months after referral, so it never left committee [S5].

against.name: Senate Republican conference
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the bipartisan backing that historically moves farm-and-nutrition bills in the Agriculture Committee [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All 12 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican signed on, and the Democratically chaired Agriculture Committee never acted on it [S4] [S5].

industries.note: Larger SNAP allotments mean more federal food dollars spent at supermarkets, corner stores, and farm stands. Retailers' gain runs alongside benefit households' gain — the money reaches both [S2] [S3].

SNAP increases are historically supported by farm-state interests because food-assistance dollars flow back to agricultural demand. Under this bill that support never translated into Senate action [S5].
